analysis.one_liner: Makes charging grossly excessive prices during emergencies illegal, with fines and disclosure rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote; after a Senate hearing in May 2024 it sat in committee until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for any seller, no matter where it sits in the supply chain, to charge a 'grossly excessive price.' During declared emergencies and disasters, large companies with market power would have been presumed to be price gouging if their prices jumped well above their pre-crisis or competitor prices, unless they could prove the increase came from real, unavoidable costs. Penalties could reach 5 percent of a company's annual revenue. Public companies would also have had to disclose in stock filings how their prices, costs, and profit margins moved during emergencies. It also included a state-level exception protecting insurance carriers and allowing resale of tickets at face value or less.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers facing sudden price spikes on essentials like groceries, gas, rent supplies, and building materials during hurricanes, pandemics, energy shortages, and other emergencies. Honest small and mid-sized sellers gain a level field, since the defense requires proving prices rose only because of uncontrollable costs, while large companies face heavier penalties and public disclosure of how much of a price hike became profit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers hit by crisis price spikes

how_it_helps.text: Makes selling any good or service at a 'grossly excessive price' illegal for every seller in the supply chain, with the FTC defining the threshold, potentially including prices at 120 percent or more of the prior six-month average.

During an 'exceptional market shock'—disasters, emergencies, power or energy failures—large companies with market power are presumed to be gouging if prices exceed pre-shock or competitor prices, and must rebut the presumption with clear and convincing evidence.

Penalties scale with company size, up to 5 percent of the ultimate parent entity's annual revenue, and the FTC gains independent authority to sue for injunctions, civil penalties, restitution, and damages on behalf of consumers.
State attorneys general can enforce the ban in federal or state court and recover restitution for their residents, and the bill leaves all stronger state price-gouging laws untouched.

Public companies must disclose in quarterly and annual securities filings how prices, costs, margins, and revenue changed during an emergency, including an explanation whenever prices rose faster than costs.

analysis.who_pays: Large retailers, fuel suppliers, building-materials suppliers, grocers, drug companies, and other sellers with revenue over $100 million, which would face new legal exposure during emergencies, mandatory profit-margin disclosures, and penalties up to 5 percent of annual revenue if they cannot prove a price increase was caused by real, uncontrollable costs.

drawbacks.text: The law applies year-round, not only during emergencies, and gives the FTC wide discretion to define 'grossly excessive'—including possibly any price at 120 percent of the prior six-month average—raising the risk of chilling legitimate price adjustments even when costs genuinely rise.

Critics in the industry argue anti-gouging rules discourage supply from flowing into shortage areas, since sellers bear legal risk for raising prices precisely when bringing scarce goods to market is most expensive.
Companies bear the burden of proving price increases were directly attributable to uncontrollable costs, which may be difficult even for businesses that did nothing wrong.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct consumer protections are strongest where price gouging is already proven to occur—during hurricanes, pandemics, and fuel shortages—and the size-based penalties and public disclosure provisions target the largest firms. The tradeoff is broader legal exposure for large sellers at all times, not just in emergencies, with outcome left to FTC rulemaking; honest sellers could face costly litigation, and some economists argue anti-gouging rules can discourage supply into shortage areas. The bill also leaves stronger state laws in place and includes carve-outs for insurance and ticket resale.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Commerce Committee, got a Senate hearing on inflation and price gouging in May 2024, and never received a committee vote or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate bill was introduced in late February 2024 and referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
In May 2024 the Banking Committee and its Economic Policy subcommittee held hearings on inflation and corporate price gouging.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended in January 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large retailers, grocers, fuel and building-materials suppliers, and other big sellers of essential goods avoided a new federal price-gouging ban, mandatory profit-margin disclosures, and penalties of up to 5 percent of annual revenue. Consumers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized all ten cosponsors, all Democrats or independents; pushed the issue through a May 2024 Senate hearing.

for.name: Senate Democratic and independent cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, including Baldwin, Casey, Sanders, Merkley, Markey, Whitehouse, Blumenthal, Fetterman, and Welch.

for.name: Senate Banking Committee and Economic Policy subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on inflation and corporate price gouging in May 2024, giving the proposal a public airing.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill; no markup or vote was scheduled in the two years it had jurisdiction.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate floor through the end of the 118th Congress and never brought the bill up; the bill drew no Republican cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents; the bill drew no Republican support and never came to a vote in a chamber Republicans controlled.

industries.industry: Large retailers, grocers, and consumer goods sellers
industries.note: Would have faced a nationwide ban on grossly excessive pricing, a presumption of gouging during emergencies, penalties up to 5 percent of revenue, and mandatory public disclosure of profit margins and pricing strategy during crises.

These industries historically see the sharpest price spikes after disasters and energy shortages; the bill targets exactly those periods, when supply shocks give large sellers leverage over captive buyers.
The disclosure requirement would have forced public companies to show investors and the public how much of a crisis-period price increase flowed to margins rather than costs.

industries.industry: Small businesses under $100 million in revenue
industries.note: Exempt from the outright ban (the affirmative defense does not apply to them) but still presumed to be gouging during emergencies if prices exceed pre-shock or competitor levels.
